# Visualisation with `ggplot2` {#sec-m1-ggplot2} ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} library(dplyr) library(ggplot2) library(scales) library(stringr) library(readxl) colunas <- c("ano", "perfil", "sh2", "pais_origem", "uf_origem", "cidade_origem", "instalacao_origem", "pais_destino", "uf_destino", "cidade_destino", "instalacao_destino", "tku") cabotagem <- readxl::read_excel("dados/cabotagem_tku_2025.xlsx", na = c("", "-")) stopifnot(ncol(cabotagem) == length(colunas)) names(cabotagem) <- colunas cabotagem <- cabotagem |> dplyr::mutate(dplyr::across(dplyr::where(is.character), str_squish)) |> dplyr::filter(tku > 0) |> dplyr::mutate(uf_origem = stringr::str_to_upper(uf_origem), uf_destino = stringr::str_to_upper(uf_destino), tku_bi = tku / 1e9) ``` ::: ## The grammar Every `ggplot2` chart has three mandatory parts: 1. **data**: a `data.frame`; 2. **aesthetic mapping** (`aes`): which column goes to the x axis, y axis, colour, size; 3. **geometry** (`geom_*`): how the data are drawn. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} por_uf <- cabotagem |> dplyr::summarise(tku_bi = sum(tku_bi), .by = uf_destino) |> dplyr::arrange(dplyr::desc(tku_bi)) ggplot(por_uf, aes(x = tku_bi, y = reorder(uf_destino, tku_bi))) + geom_col() ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![Minimal structure of a chart](m1-07-ggplot2_files/figure-html/fig-primeiro-1.png){#fig-primeiro width=1200} ::: ::: Layers are added with `+`. From there everything is refinement: scales, labels, theme. ## The geometries you will use ### Bars ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} ggplot(por_uf, aes(x = tku_bi, y = reorder(uf_destino, tku_bi))) + geom_col(fill = "#1a5b8a") + geom_text(aes(label = scales::number(tku_bi, accuracy = 0.1)), hjust = -0.15, size = 3) + scale_x_continuous(expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.12))) + labs( title = "Coastal shipping: TKU by destination state", subtitle = "Billions of tonne-kilometres, 2025", x = "TKU (billion t·km)", y = NULL, caption = "Source: ANTAQ, Estatístico Aquaviário." ) + theme_minimal(base_size = 11) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![Coastal shipping TKU by destination state (2025)](m1-07-ggplot2_files/figure-html/fig-barras-1.png){#fig-barras width=1200} ::: ::: Note two technical choices: **horizontal** bars (long names stay readable) and `reorder()` (orders by value, not alphabetically). Use `geom_col()` when the height is in a column of the data, and `geom_bar()` when you want `ggplot2` to count the rows. ### Grouped and stacked bars ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} por_perfil <- cabotagem |> dplyr::summarise(tku_bi = sum(tku_bi), .by = c(uf_destino, perfil)) |> dplyr::filter(uf_destino %in% por_uf$uf_destino[1:8]) ggplot(por_perfil, aes(x = tku_bi, y = reorder(uf_destino, tku_bi), fill = perfil)) + geom_col() + # stacked (default) scale_fill_brewer(palette = "Blues", direction = -1) + labs(x = "TKU (billion t·km)", y = NULL, fill = "Cargo profile") + theme_minimal(base_size = 11) + theme(legend.position = "bottom") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![Composition of TKU by cargo profile](m1-07-ggplot2_files/figure-html/fig-barras-perfil-1.png){#fig-barras-perfil width=1200} ::: ::: Switching to proportions, with `position = "fill"`, the chart now reads as composition: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} ggplot(por_perfil, aes(x = tku_bi, y = reorder(uf_destino, tku_bi), fill = perfil)) + geom_col(position = "fill") + scale_x_continuous(labels = scales::percent_format(accuracy = 1)) + scale_fill_brewer(palette = "Blues", direction = -1) + labs(x = NULL, y = NULL, fill = NULL) + theme_minimal(base_size = 11) + theme(legend.position = "bottom") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![Share of each cargo profile in destination TKU](m1-07-ggplot2_files/figure-html/fig-barras-fill-1.png){#fig-barras-fill width=1200} ::: ::: `position = "dodge"` puts the bars side by side. ### Scatter plot ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} resumo_uf <- cabotagem |> dplyr::summarise(ligacoes = dplyr::n(), tku_bi = sum(tku_bi), .by = uf_destino) ggplot(resumo_uf, aes(x = ligacoes, y = tku_bi)) + geom_point(size = 3, alpha = 0.7, colour = "#1a5b8a") + ggrepel::geom_text_repel(aes(label = uf_destino), size = 3) + geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE, linewidth = 0.5, colour = "grey40", linetype = "dashed") + labs(x = "Number of OD links", y = "TKU (billion t·km)") + theme_minimal(base_size = 11) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![Number of links versus total TKU by destination state](m1-07-ggplot2_files/figure-html/fig-scatter-1.png){#fig-scatter width=1200} ::: ::: ### Histogram, density and cumulative distribution For very skewed variables, such as TKU, the logarithmic axis is the difference between an unreadable chart and an informative one. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} ggplot(cabotagem, aes(x = tku)) + geom_histogram(bins = 30, fill = "#1a5b8a", colour = "white") + scale_x_log10(labels = scales::label_log()) + labs(x = "TKU per link (t·km, log scale)", y = "Number of links") + theme_minimal(base_size = 11) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![Distribution of TKU per OD link (log scale)](m1-07-ggplot2_files/figure-html/fig-hist-1.png){#fig-hist width=1200} ::: ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} g1 <- ggplot(cabotagem, aes(x = tku)) + geom_density(fill = "#1a5b8a", alpha = 0.3) + scale_x_log10() + labs(x = "TKU (log)", y = "Density") + theme_minimal(base_size = 10) g2 <- ggplot(cabotagem, aes(x = tku)) + stat_ecdf(geom = "step", linewidth = 0.8, colour = "#1a5b8a") + scale_x_log10() + scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent_format()) + labs(x = "TKU (log)", y = "Cumulative links") + theme_minimal(base_size = 10) patchwork::wrap_plots(g1, g2) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![Density (left) and cumulative distribution (right)](m1-07-ggplot2_files/figure-html/fig-dens-cdf-1.png){#fig-dens-cdf width=1200} ::: ::: The cumulative curve directly answers a planning question: *how many pairs concentrate what fraction of the TKU?* ### Boxplot ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} ggplot(cabotagem, aes(x = tku, y = reorder(perfil, tku, FUN = median))) + geom_boxplot(outlier.alpha = 0.4, fill = "grey95") + scale_x_log10(labels = scales::label_log()) + labs(x = "TKU per link (log)", y = NULL) + theme_minimal(base_size = 11) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![TKU per link, by cargo profile](m1-07-ggplot2_files/figure-html/fig-box-1.png){#fig-box width=1200} ::: ::: ### Lines: time series ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} serie <- data.frame( ano = 2015:2025, tku_bi = c(24.1, 23.4, 25.8, 27.2, 28.9, 27.1, 30.4, 32.2, 33.8, 35.1, 36.4) ) ggplot(serie, aes(x = ano, y = tku_bi)) + geom_line(linewidth = 0.9, colour = "#1a5b8a") + geom_point(size = 2, colour = "#1a5b8a") + scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(2015, 2025, 2)) + labs(x = NULL, y = "TKU (billion t·km)") + theme_minimal(base_size = 11) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![Example time series with made-up data](m1-07-ggplot2_files/figure-html/fig-linha-1.png){#fig-linha width=1200} ::: ::: ## Scales, labels and formats The `scales` package handles number formatting. Its defaults follow the English convention (decimal point, comma for thousands); for reports in Portuguese, the Brazilian convention is the opposite, and the arguments `big.mark` and `decimal.mark` switch it: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} scales::number(1234567.891, big.mark = ",", accuracy = 0.01) # English #> [1] "1,234,567.89" scales::number(1234567.891, big.mark = ".", decimal.mark = ",", accuracy = 0.01) # Brazilian #> [1] "1.234.567,89" scales::percent(0.1234, accuracy = 0.1) #> [1] "12.3%" scales::label_number(scale = 1e-9, suffix = " bn")(8332538649) #> [1] "8 bn" scales::comma(1234567) #> [1] "1,234,567" ``` ::: Applying it to the axis: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} ggplot(por_uf |> dplyr::slice_head(n = 8), aes(x = tku_bi, y = reorder(uf_destino, tku_bi))) + geom_col(fill = "#1a5b8a") + scale_x_continuous( labels = scales::label_number(big.mark = ",", accuracy = 0.1) ) + labs(x = "TKU (billion t·km)", y = NULL) + theme_minimal(base_size = 11) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![Axis with formatted numbers](m1-07-ggplot2_files/figure-html/fig-escalas-1.png){#fig-escalas width=1200} ::: ::: Other useful scales: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0, 40)) # limits scale_y_continuous(transform = "log10") # transformation scale_x_date(date_labels = "%b/%Y", date_breaks = "3 months") # dates scale_fill_viridis_c() # continuous, perceptually uniform scale_fill_viridis_d() # discrete scale_colour_manual(values = c("Rodoviário" = "#1a5b8a", "Cabotagem" = "#e07b39")) coord_flip() # swaps the axes coord_cartesian(xlim = c(0, 10)) # crops without dropping data ``` ::: ::: {.callout-warning} `scale_x_continuous(limits = ...)` **removes** the observations outside the limit (and affects means and smoothers); `coord_cartesian(xlim = ...)` only zooms. To crop the view, use `coord_cartesian()`. ::: ## Factors: controlling the order ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} cabotagem |> dplyr::summarise(tku_bi = sum(tku_bi), .by = perfil) |> dplyr::mutate(perfil = forcats::fct_reorder(perfil, tku_bi)) |> ggplot(aes(x = tku_bi, y = perfil)) + geom_col(fill = "#1a5b8a") + labs(x = "TKU (billion t·km)", y = NULL) + theme_minimal(base_size = 11) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![Explicit order of the categories](m1-07-ggplot2_files/figure-html/fig-forcats-1.png){#fig-forcats width=1200} ::: ::: `forcats` functions worth memorising: `fct_reorder()` (orders by another variable), `fct_infreq()` (by frequency), `fct_rev()` (reverses), `fct_lump_n()` (groups the small categories into "Other") and `fct_relevel()` (manual order). ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} cabotagem |> dplyr::mutate(sh2_top = forcats::fct_lump_n(sh2, n = 5, w = tku)) |> dplyr::summarise(tku_bi = sum(tku_bi), .by = sh2_top) |> dplyr::arrange(dplyr::desc(tku_bi)) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} `````{=html}
````` ::: ::: ## Panels (`facet`) ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} cabotagem |> dplyr::summarise(tku_bi = sum(tku_bi), .by = c(perfil, uf_destino)) |> dplyr::slice_max(tku_bi, n = 5, by = perfil) |> ggplot(aes(x = tku_bi, y = reorder(uf_destino, tku_bi))) + geom_col(fill = "#1a5b8a") + facet_wrap(~perfil, scales = "free") + labs(x = "TKU (billion t·km)", y = NULL) + theme_minimal(base_size = 10) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![One panel per cargo profile](m1-07-ggplot2_files/figure-html/fig-facet-1.png){#fig-facet width=1200} ::: ::: `scales = "free"` gives each panel its own scale: good for comparing **shape**, bad for comparing **magnitude**. Choose deliberately. ## Annotations ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} maior <- cabotagem |> dplyr::slice_max(tku, n = 1) ggplot(resumo_uf, aes(x = ligacoes, y = tku_bi)) + geom_point(colour = "grey60", size = 2.5) + geom_point(data = resumo_uf |> dplyr::filter(uf_destino == maior$uf_destino), colour = "#e07b39", size = 4) + annotate("text", x = 30, y = max(resumo_uf$tku_bi) * 0.95, label = stringr::str_glue("Largest link: {maior$cidade_origem} > {maior$cidade_destino}"), hjust = 0, size = 3.2) + geom_hline(yintercept = mean(resumo_uf$tku_bi), linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey50") + labs(x = "OD links", y = "TKU (billion t·km)") + theme_minimal(base_size = 11) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![Highlighting a specific point](m1-07-ggplot2_files/figure-html/fig-anotacao-1.png){#fig-anotacao width=1200} ::: ::: ## Themes and visual identity ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} theme_minimal(); theme_bw(); theme_classic(); theme_void() ``` ::: To standardise every chart in a report, define the theme once: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} tema_mt <- function(base_size = 11) { theme_minimal(base_size = base_size) + theme( plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = rel(1.15)), plot.subtitle = element_text(colour = "grey35"), plot.caption = element_text(colour = "grey45", size = rel(0.8)), panel.grid.minor = element_blank(), legend.position = "bottom" ) } theme_set(tema_mt()) ``` ::: From here on, every chart in the document inherits this theme. ## 2D frequency maps When many points overlap (typical of GPS coordinates or OD pairs), two-dimensional histograms show density instead of stacked points. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} cabotagem |> dplyr::left_join(resumo_uf |> dplyr::select(uf_destino, ligacoes), by = "uf_destino") |> ggplot(aes(x = ligacoes, y = tku)) + geom_bin2d(bins = 20) + scale_y_log10() + scale_fill_viridis_c(option = "magma", direction = -1) + labs(x = "Links of the destination state", y = "TKU of the link (log)", fill = "Number of\nlinks") + tema_mt() ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![Density of links by TKU band and number of links of the state](m1-07-ggplot2_files/figure-html/fig-bin2d-1.png){#fig-bin2d width=1200} ::: ::: `geom_hex()` does the same with hexagonal cells (requires the `hexbin` package). In module 2 this same logic appears over geographic space, with hexagon grids. ## Class breaks: Jenks and alternatives When classifying values into bands (the mandatory step of any thematic map), the break method completely changes how the result reads. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} library(classInt) valores <- resumo_uf$tku_bi quebras_jenks <- classInt::classIntervals(valores, n = 5, style = "jenks") quebras_quant <- classInt::classIntervals(valores, n = 5, style = "quantile") quebras_iguais <- classInt::classIntervals(valores, n = 5, style = "equal") round(quebras_jenks$brks, 2) #> [1] 0.00 5.70 23.14 30.70 46.91 58.35 round(quebras_quant$brks, 2) #> [1] 0.00 0.45 8.07 18.78 27.64 58.35 round(quebras_iguais$brks, 2) #> [1] 0.00 11.67 23.34 35.01 46.68 58.35 ``` ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} classificar <- function(x, estilo) { q <- classInt::classIntervals(x, n = 5, style = estilo) cut(x, breaks = q$brks, include.lowest = TRUE, dig.lab = 2) } resumo_uf |> dplyr::mutate( Jenks = classificar(tku_bi, "jenks"), Quantile = classificar(tku_bi, "quantile"), `Equal intervals` = classificar(tku_bi, "equal") ) |> tidyr::pivot_longer(c(Jenks, Quantile, `Equal intervals`), names_to = "metodo", values_to = "classe") |> ggplot(aes(x = 1, y = reorder(uf_destino, tku_bi), fill = as.integer(classe))) + geom_tile() + facet_wrap(~metodo) + scale_fill_viridis_c(option = "viridis", breaks = 1:5) + labs(x = NULL, y = NULL, fill = "Class") + theme_minimal(base_size = 9) + theme(axis.text.x = element_blank(), panel.grid = element_blank()) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![The same states classified by three break methods](m1-07-ggplot2_files/figure-html/fig-jenks-1.png){#fig-jenks width=1200} ::: ::: | Method | When to use | |:--|:--| | `jenks` (natural breaks) | skewed data; maximises the difference between classes | | `quantile` | guarantees the same number of units per class; good for rankings | | `equal` | bands of equal width; good when the scale has its own meaning | | `pretty` | round breaks, readable in a legend | | `fisher` | equivalent to Jenks, faster on large datasets | ::: {.callout-note} Keep this block: in module 5 it comes back applied to choropleth maps with `sf`, and the choice of method will be justified in the final report. ::: ## Saving charts ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} g <- ggplot(por_uf, aes(tku_bi, reorder(uf_destino, tku_bi))) + geom_col() ggsave("resultados/tku_uf.png", g, width = 18, height = 12, units = "cm", dpi = 300) ggsave("resultados/tku_uf.pdf", g, width = 18, height = 12, units = "cm") # vector ggsave("resultados/tku_uf.svg", g, width = 18, height = 12, units = "cm") # editable ``` ::: For institutional reports, prefer **PDF or SVG**: the chart does not lose quality when enlarged or printed. Set the dimensions in centimetres, thinking of the usable width of the page (about 16 cm on A4 with standard margins).
